accroche: Aladdin and Ali Baba come from no Arabic manuscript: they are the oral memories of a Syrian storyteller whom the translator never cited.
contenu_vulgarise:
Paris, spring 1709. Antoine Galland, orientalist and translator, has already published seven volumes of *Les Mille et Une Nuits* (*The Thousand and One Nights*), but the Arabic manuscript he is working from stops short: he has no more stories to translate. A mutual friend then introduces him to a young Syrian passing through the capital, Hanna Diyab, a Maronite Christian from Aleppo, who has come to France after a long journey across the Mediterranean. Diyab knows dozens of tales learned in his childhood. He tells them to Galland, in French, over several meetings.

## A Translator, a Storyteller, No Name

Galland's journal dates these meetings precisely: on March 25, 1709, a first summary of tales; on May 5, the story of the wonderful lamp, which will become Aladdin; on May 27, Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves. A dozen or so other stories follow until June, about fifteen in all. Ten of them, including these two, appear in the last four volumes of Galland's *Mille et Une Nuits*, published in 1712 and then in 1717. None comes from an earlier Arabic manuscript: they are tales that scholars now call “orphans,” with no source other than the memory of a man whom Galland never cites in his printed volumes.

Aladdin and Ali Baba, the two most widely read stories in the world under the name of the *Thousand and One Nights*, thus never existed in an Arabic manuscript before that spring of 1709. They exist because a young man passing through Paris remembered them, and because a translator short of material wrote down what he retained of them.

## Three Centuries to Recover a Voice

Diyab, for his part, left his own trace. Decades later, he wrote down in Arabic the story of his own journey, from his Mediterranean to Paris, where he describes meeting an old man in charge of a library of Arabic books (Galland, never named either, by way of payback). This manuscript sleeps in the Vatican Library, under the shelfmark Sbath 254, identified only in 1993. It had to wait until 2015 to appear in French, under the title *D'Alep à Paris* (*From Aleppo to Paris*), and then 2021 for a complete English translation. Three hundred and six years separate the spring when Diyab told Aladdin to Galland from the first time his own account, in his own words, becomes readable.

repere.texte: Of the twelve volumes of Antoine Galland's Thousand and One Nights, published between 1704 and 1717, the last four contain ten tales that come from no earlier Arabic manuscript: among them, Aladdin and Ali Baba, transmitted orally by Hanna Diyab alone in 1709.
repere.source: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Bibliothèques d'Orient

carte.punch: Aladdin and Ali Baba have no Arabic manuscript earlier than 1709. Galland did not name his storyteller.
carte.idee: Aladdin and Ali Baba exist in no Arabic manuscript earlier than 1709. They are the oral memories of Hanna Diyab, a Syrian storyteller whom Antoine Galland met in Paris and never named in his printed Thousand and One Nights.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Robyn Creswell, “On the Road,” The New York Review of Books, 2021
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: On the rediscovery of Hanna Diyab as an author in his own right, based on his own travel account.

quiz.question: Why do Aladdin and Ali Baba appear in no Arabic manuscript earlier than 1709?
choix: Because they are tales made up from scratch by Antoine Galland, with no source at all
Because they belong to an Egyptian manuscript tradition that Galland discovered only after 1717
Because they come only from the oral memories of a Syrian storyteller whom Galland met in Paris, without his having read them in a manuscript
Because Ottoman censorship had removed them from the manuscripts in circulation before the 18th century
quiz.explication: Galland invented nothing (he is not the author of the tales), and no late Egyptian manuscript or Ottoman censorship comes into play: no earlier Arabic manuscript contains these stories. They come from the oral memories of Hanna Diyab, a Syrian storyteller met in Paris in the spring of 1709, whom Galland wrote down without ever naming him in his printed volumes.

quiz_supplementaire.question: On what date does Hanna Diyab tell Galland the story that will become Aladdin?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Galland's journal dates these meetings precisely: on March 25, 1709 a first summary of tales, on May 5 the story of the wonderful lamp that will become Aladdin, and on May 27 Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where is the manuscript in which Hanna Diyab tells, in Arabic, the story of his own journey kept today?
choix: At the Bibliothèque nationale de France, in Paris
At the library of the University of Aleppo, in Syria
At the Vatican Library, under the shelfmark Sbath 254
It was lost and survives only as partial copies
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Diyab's autobiographical manuscript sleeps in the Vatican Library, under the shelfmark Sbath 254, identified only in 1993; it had to wait until 2015 to appear in French, and then 2021 for a complete English translation.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where does Hanna Diyab, the storyteller from whom Galland has the tales of Aladdin and Ali Baba, come from?
choix: From Cairo, Egypt: he is a merchant who came to sell manuscripts in Paris
From Baghdad, Iraq: he is a scholar invited by the Académie française
From Tunis, Tunisia: he is an interpreter employed by the French embassy
From Aleppo, Syria: he is a Maronite Christian who arrived in France after a long journey
quiz_supplementaire.explication: A mutual friend introduces Galland to a young Syrian passing through Paris, Hanna Diyab, a Maronite Christian from Aleppo, who arrived in France after a long journey across the Mediterranean.
